title: Class 3: Skills, and cut the cord

series.title: Physical AI Lab: Build a Robot Desk Assistant (4 evenings)
series.summary: Four Tuesday evenings, one robot, with a study hall before each one for catching up and asking questions. Evening 1: build a robot that talks in a Deepgram voice and moves its mouth, powered by your laptop, and write its personality. Evening 2: give the servos their own power, add moving eyes, and give it several personalities you switch between by voice. Evening 3: skills (function calls) and cutting the cord: drive it from your phone over Bluetooth, or move it onto a Raspberry Pi. Evening 4: show and tell. No coding needed.

summary: Give your robot skills, real function calls that answer with real data: Muni trips, timers, notes, look-ups, the weather. Then get it off the laptop: drive it from your phone over Bluetooth (Android in Chrome, or iPhone with the free Bluefy app), or move its brain onto a Raspberry Pi.
detail: First, skills. Each one is a function call: the agent decides when it needs one, your page runs it and hands back a real answer. Ask how to get to the Ferry Building and it tells you which Muni bus to catch, where, and when the next one comes. Then cut the cord. Until now the laptop has been the brain: the mic, the connection to the Deepgram Voice Agent, the speaker. Way A, Bluetooth: open this page on your phone and it sends the same little commands to the Pico by radio instead of a cable, while the robot sits on a charger or BreadVolt. It works on Android; iPhone with Bluefy is still being tested. Way B, a Raspberry Pi you set up at home rides inside the robot with a speakerphone and a battery, and opens this same page. Same personalities, same skills either way. Got time left? Add extras: eyebrows, a neck.
outcome: A robot with the skills you picked, answering with real data, that talks and moves with no laptop attached: driven by your phone over Bluetooth, or by a Raspberry Pi inside it.
artifact: A wireless talking robot with function-call skills.
prereqs: Your robot from Evening 2, your laptop and your Deepgram key.
Know a few places you go in San Francisco: you'll ask your robot how to get there.

For Bluetooth, bring your phone, charged. Android: use Chrome. iPhone: install the free Bluefy app from the App Store before class (Safari and Chrome on iPhone can't use Bluetooth from a web page). Optional: a small Bluetooth speaker, so the voice comes from the robot.

Doing the Pi upgrade? Bring a Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 (2 GB or more) with its memory card and power supply, set up at home as below, a USB speakerphone (any brand, for example an EMEET M0 Plus), and a battery pack. No Pi? Skip the rest of this list.
Battery: a USB power bank of 20,000 mAh with a USB-C port rated 30 W or more, and a second USB port for the servos. It runs a Pi robot for about 6 hours. A smaller 10,000 mAh bank works for about 3.

Optional upgrade list, to match the instructor's robot. Buy these yourself: ☐ Raspberry Pi 5 (4 GB) ☐ Raspberry Pi 5 Active Cooler ☐ 32 GB microSD card ☐ Official Raspberry Pi 27 W USB-C power supply, for setting up at home ☐ USB speakerphone, for example an EMEET M0 Plus ☐ Anker 20,000 mAh power bank with a USB-C port rated 30 W or more.

1. On your computer, install Raspberry Pi Imager from raspberrypi.com/software and use it to put Raspberry Pi OS (64-bit, with desktop) on the memory card. In its settings, add a username and password and the Hub's wifi from your event email.
2. Start the Pi once with a screen, keyboard and mouse, and finish the welcome steps.
3. Turn on Raspberry Pi Connect (its icon is in the top bar) and sign in with a free Raspberry Pi ID. On your laptop, check you can see the Pi's screen at connect.raspberrypi.com.
4. Plug in your speakerphone, check the Pi plays sound through it, then open Chromium and visit this page once, so it's ready.

slides.title: Class 3: Skills, and cut the cord
bullets: First half: skills. Real function calls that answer with real data.
Second half: get it off the laptop. Your phone over Bluetooth, or a Raspberry Pi.
Time left? Extras: eyebrows, a neck.
slides.note: Show of hands: Android? iPhone with Bluefy? Brought a Pi? Seat Pi people together so helpers can work the tables, and keep Bluetooth people a little spread out.

slides.title: What a function call is
bullets: You describe a function to the agent: its name, what it does, what it needs.
When the conversation calls for it, the agent asks your page to run it.
Your page does the real work: asks Muni, sets a timer, saves a note.
The answer goes back to the agent, and it says it in its own voice.
slides.note: Two minutes. They used two already in Evening 2: crossing the eyes and switching personality. Show the Tool lines in the transcript and the Code panel: the skills you tick become the functions in the agent's settings.

slides.title: Pick its skills
bullets: Open Skills (function calls) and tick the ones you want:
Check the weather · Deepgram events in San Francisco · Timers
Remember notes · Plan a Muni trip · Look things up · Dice, coins and picking
Each one you tick shows a Try: line. Say it and watch the Tool lines.
slides.note: Fewer skills keep a robot focused. Push people to choose what fits their robot, not tick everything. Notes are kept in that browser only. Look things up uses Wikipedia, and says so when there's no article instead of guessing.

slides.title: Where to, and which bus?
bullets: Tick Plan a Muni trip.
Ask: how do I get to the Ferry Building?
It tells you the line, where to catch it, which way it's heading, and when the next one comes.
Trips start from The Hub at 505 Howard, unless you say where you're starting from.
slides.note: Live arrival times come from 511.org; stops and routes come from Muni's published timetable. Short trips get "just walk". The credit line under the skills list is required by Muni's data licence; leave it there.

slides.title: Give it a job
bullets: Pick a job: Hub concierge, study buddy, game-night host, commute helper.
Give one of your personalities that job, and tick only the skills it needs.
Tell it, in its personality, when to use each skill.
Test it with a partner playing someone who needs help.
slides.note: Good pairs: a commute helper with Muni and the weather; a game host with dice and timers; a study buddy with look-ups, notes and timers.

slides.title: Two ways to get off the laptop
bullets: The laptop has been the brain: mic, Voice Agent, speaker. Going wireless means moving the brain.
A · Your phone over Bluetooth: about $0–20, works on Android, iPhone being tested.
B · A Raspberry Pi inside: about $130–170, bring your own, proven.
Both keep the Pico, servos and breadboard exactly as wired in Evening 2.
slides.note: Neither? Stay on the laptop, add extras, and polish for show and tell.

slides.title: What each robot needs for the cord-cutting
bullets: Bluetooth: ☐ your phone, charged (Android with Chrome, or iPhone with Bluefy installed)
Bluetooth: ☐ 1 × USB-A to micro-USB cable, Pico to the charger (on the table) ☐ a 2-port USB charger, or your BreadVolt
Bluetooth, optional: ☐ a small Bluetooth speaker for inside the robot
Pi: ☐ your Raspberry Pi 4 or 5, set up at home ☐ your USB speakerphone ☐ your battery pack, charged
Pi: ☐ 1 × USB-A to micro-USB data cable, for the Pico ☐ 1 × short cable from the battery to the Pi's USB-C port ☐ Velcro strips or tape
Extras: ☐ spare MG90S servos for eyebrows or a neck (helper table)
Bring: your laptop and your Deepgram key
slides.note: Charger ports: a Bluetooth robot on a charger uses 2 ports (Pico + servo lead), so a 6-port charger serves 3. Count them before class. USB-C to micro-USB cables don't fit a USB-A charger, so have USB-A to micro-USB cables on every table. Every Pico loaded since Evening 1 already has the Bluetooth program; a Pico loaded before Nov 24 needs the current main.py at the helper table. Pi helper table: a setup station with a screen, keyboard, mouse and micro-HDMI cable; spare cables; one or two spare charged batteries.

slides.title: Who does what now
bullets: Your phone is the brain: it runs this page, hears you, talks to Deepgram and speaks.
Bluetooth replaces the USB cable. It sends short commands: M35 = mouth to 35 degrees, X = cross your eyes.
The Pico W is still the controller, and the servos are wired exactly as before.
The robot never needs wifi. Only your phone uses the internet.
slides.note: The voice comes out of the phone: prop it behind the robot, or pair a small Bluetooth speaker and put it inside. A Bluetooth speaker plays a little late, so the mouth can run slightly ahead of the voice.

slides.title: Power it from the wall
bullets: Unplug the Pico's cable from your laptop and plug it into a USB charger instead.
The servos stay on their own power: the 2-pin lead in the charger's second port, or your BreadVolt.
Nothing changes on the breadboard. Pin 40 stays empty.
slides.note: This is exactly how it was tested: Pico on a wall charger, servos on a BreadVolt, Android phone as the brain, no laptop. Power check: the Pico draws about 0.1 A, three servos about 0.9 A, and each charger port gives about 2.4 A.

slides.title: Or: everything on the BreadVolt
bullets: No wall at all: one extra jumper from the + row to VSYS (pin 39) powers the Pico from the BreadVolt.
Unplug the Pico's USB cable when you run it this way. Never both.
The BreadVolt gives about 1.5 A: enough for the Pico and three servos.
slides.note: Advanced option: the wall-charger way is the one we've tested. Make sure the BreadVolt is set to 5 V before adding the VSYS jumper.

slides.title: Connect from your phone
bullets: Android: open this page in Chrome, with Bluetooth and Location on. iPhone: open it in the Bluefy app.
Paste your key, then tap Connect by Bluetooth and pick your robot: Robot- plus the four characters on the sticker on your box.
Set the mouth and tick your eyes and skills again: they're saved per phone.
Recreate your personalities, or copy them across from your laptop's Code panel. Then start talking.
slides.note: Every Pico has its own name, from its serial number, so 50 robots don't get mixed up. Lost sticker? Plug the Pico into a laptop and open Thonny: it prints BLUETOOTH NAME Robot-XXXX when it starts. If a phone can't find its robot in a crowded room, move closer and try again, or fall back to the cable. Nobody leaves without a working robot.

slides.title: Plug in the Pi
bullets: Speakerphone into a blue USB port on the Pi.
Unplug the Pico from your laptop and plug it into another blue port, with the USB-A cable.
Battery: the Pi goes in the USB-C port, and the servo power lead goes in the other port.
Fix the Pi and battery inside the robot, on the floor at the back, with velcro or tape. Cut a small notch for the charging cable.
slides.note: Done when: the Pi's light flickers and the speakerphone lights up. The battery is the heaviest part, so low and at the back keeps the robot from tipping. Tip: tape the back flap on one side only, like a hinge, so you can open it to charge or fix things.

slides.title: Open the Pi from your laptop
bullets: On your laptop, go to connect.raspberrypi.com and open your Pi's screen.
On the Pi, open Chromium and go to this lesson page.
slides.note: If someone's Pi didn't come up on the wifi, send them to the setup station. Connect's screen sharing can't paste reliably; to get the key across, type it, or a helper can copy it on with SSH.

slides.title: Set it up on the Pi
bullets: Paste your Deepgram key and connect the robot, like Class 1.
Pick the speakerphone if Chromium asks for a microphone.
Set the mouth again, and tick your eyes and skills again: they're saved per computer.
Recreate your personalities, or copy them across from your laptop's Code panel.
Start talking.
slides.note: Profiles, skills and mouth settings live in each browser, so the Pi starts fresh. Speakerphones cancel their own echo well, so barge-in can usually stay on.

slides.title: Add an extra
bullets: Eyebrows: a servo above each eye, on the same + and − rows.
A neck: the program already drives one on GP14 (pin 19).
Count your servos against your power: a BreadVolt feeds about 3, a charger port about 5.
Three or more servos: a 470–1000 µF capacitor across + and − helps.
slides.note: Extras are for people who finished early. The neck uses the robot page's neck controls. Eyebrows need new firmware commands, so treat them as decoration for now unless a helper has the eyebrow program ready.

slides.title: Walk away with it
bullets: Bluetooth: close your laptop, walk across the room with your phone and keep talking. The robot stays on its charger.
Pi: close the Pi on your laptop, pick the robot up and carry it to another table. Keep talking.
Still on the laptop? Show your robot to a wireless builder, and hear theirs.
Ask it a skill question while you walk: how do I get home from here?
slides.note: Done when: it holds a conversation with no laptop attached. Bluetooth reaches about one room.

slides.title: Evening 4: show and tell
bullets: Show off your robot and everything it can do.
Bring it with its brain: your laptop, your phone (charged) or your Pi (charged).
Invite a friend: guests are welcome.

flow.title: Cut the cord: pick your way
Way B: move it onto a Pi
Run your robot
flow.note: Laptop: as usual. Bluetooth: open this page on your phone (Chrome on Android, Bluefy on iPhone) and press Connect by Bluetooth. Pi: open it in Chromium on the Pi.

flow.title: Extras, walk test and next evening

troubleshooting: It makes up an answer instead of using a skill: check the skill is ticked, then ask more directly ("check the weather in Paris").
Muni says it can't find a place: give a street address or a well-known place in San Francisco.
Muni gives a line but no time: the live feed didn't answer. It suggests the Muni app instead; try again in a minute.
A timer didn't go off: timers only run while this page is open and the robot is connected.
Its notes are gone: notes are kept in this browser. A different laptop, phone or browser starts empty.
There's no Connect by Bluetooth button, or it does nothing: on iPhone you're in Safari or Chrome, so open the page in Bluefy instead. On Android, use Chrome.

Your robot's name doesn't show up: turn on Bluetooth (and Location on Android), check the Pico has power from the charger, and move closer. Only one phone can connect at a time: is someone else connected to it?
No robot names appear at all: the Pico has an old program without Bluetooth. Take it to the helper table for the current main.py.
The wrong robot moved: you picked a neighbour's name. Disconnect and pick the name on your box's sticker.
Connected by Bluetooth but the mouth won't move: the servos have no power. Switch the BreadVolt on, or plug the 2-pin lead into the charger.
Bluetooth keeps dropping: stay in the same room as the robot and keep the page open with the screen on. Phones cut connections when the screen locks.
The Pi isn't on the wifi, or Connect can't find it: take it to the setup station and fix the wifi with a screen and keyboard.
Connect robot shows nothing on the Pi: the Pico cable is charge-only. Swap it for a data cable.
The robot can't hear you: in Chromium, click the lock icon and pick your speakerphone as the microphone.
No sound: set your speakerphone as the Pi's audio output in the speaker menu at the top right.

The sound is choppy or the speakerphone keeps disconnecting: the Pi is short of power for its USB ports. Use the battery's highest-power USB-C port and a short, thick cable, or plug in the Pi's own power supply for now.
The Pi shows a lightning bolt or restarts: the battery port can't keep up. Try the other port or a thicker cable.
The battery switches itself off: some power banks sleep on low current. Press its button to wake it.
Chromium shows an Unlock Keyring box and pages won't load: press Cancel, then ask a helper to switch the keyring off.

The page says the robot reset while talking: a servo is pulling power from the Pico. Check every red wire goes to the + row, the BreadVolt is switched on or the power lead is in a charger, nothing is on pin 40, and the ground jumper to pin 23 is in.
Connect robot does nothing at all: you're not in Chrome. Open the page in Chrome (or Chromium on a Raspberry Pi).
Another program is using the port: quit Thonny and close other tabs with this page, unplug the Pico, plug it back in, and connect again.
It cuts you off: raise Patience. It's slow to answer: lower it.
It talks to itself, or stops mid-sentence for no reason: it's hearing its own voice. Switch off Let me interrupt it (barge-in), or move the laptop away from the robot's speaker.
Deepgram stopped the session: check the key was pasted whole, and that the account has credit.
